questions.q: What is the immediate reason the pilot decides to fly his old Dakota straight into the storm clouds instead of turning back to Paris?
questions.a: The pilot decides to fly into the storm because he wants to reach England in time for a big English breakfast with his family. A wrong answer (e.g., "he was ordered to" or "he didn't see the clouds") reveals the student cannot distinguish between external compulsion and the pilot's internal motivation (desire for home/comfort), which is crucial for understanding his responsibility for the ensuing crisis.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why the pilot's compass and radio stop working when he enters the storm clouds.
questions.a: The storm clouds create atmospheric interference (static electricity, turbulence) that disrupts the magnetic compass and radio signals. A wrong answer (e.g., "the instruments were old/broken") shows the student misses the cause-effect link: the *storm itself* causes the failure, emphasizing nature's power over technology — a key theme. If they say "the black aeroplane jammed them," they confuse chronological order (instruments fail *before* the black plane appears).

questions.q: The narrator says: "I was lost in the storm. Suddenly, I saw a black aeroplane... The pilot of the black aeroplane waved his hand... 'Follow me,' he was saying." Apply the concept of 'turning point' to explain how this moment changes the direction of the narrative.
questions.a: Before this moment, the narrative trajectory is toward disaster (certain death by crash or fuel exhaustion). The black aeroplane's appearance introduces an external saviour, shifting the genre from realistic survival to mystery/supernatural. The pilot's agency shifts from "fighting instruments" to "blindly following." A weak answer merely describes the event without naming the structural shift (e.g., "the plane helped him"). The correct application identifies the turning point as the pivot from *helplessness* to *guided hope*.

questions.q: Compare the pilot's physical surroundings *inside* the storm clouds (paragraphs 3-4) with his surroundings *after* he follows the black aeroplane out of the clouds (paragraph 7). What contrast does the author create?
questions.a: Inside: "everything was black," "could not see anything," "compass turning round and round," "radio dead" — sensory deprivation, chaos, instrument failure. Outside: "two long straight lines of lights," "an airport," "runway" — order, visibility, safety, human civilisation. The contrast highlights the storm as a liminal space (chaos/death) vs. the airport as structured life. A poor answer lists details without synthesising the *symbolic contrast* (chaos vs. order).

questions.q: The pilot lands safely and asks the control tower woman: "Where is the other pilot? I want to thank him." She replies: "There was no other plane... yours was the only one on radar." Evaluate the reliability of the narrator's perception. Did the black aeroplane *really* exist?
questions.a: The text deliberately leaves this ambiguous. The narrator *experiences* it vividly (sees the pilot's face, waves, follows), but radar (objective technology) detects nothing. A strong evaluation argues: "The story operates on two levels — the pilot's subjective reality (where the plane was real and saved him) and objective reality (radar shows nothing). The author forces the reader to choose between a supernatural explanation (guardian angel, hallucination from hypoxia) or a psychological one (the pilot's subconscious projected a guide)." A weak answer picks one side dogmatically ("it was a ghost" or "he was dreaming") without acknowledging the textual evidence for *both* interpretations.

questions.q: Write a 50-word diary entry from the pilot's perspective *that night*, capturing his confusion about the black aeroplane. Use first-person narration and sensory details.
questions.a: A strong entry: "October 12. Landed safe. But I'm shaking. That black plane — no lights, no radar trace — guided me down. The control room says I was alone. Did I imagine the pilot's face? His wave? The storm took my compass, but who gave me back my life? Breakfast tastes strange tonight." Criteria: first-person, references radar discrepancy, includes sensory/emotional detail, under 50 words. A poor entry writes in third person, omits the radar contradiction, or exceeds length.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: This topic covers the plot ______ and atmospheric setting of the second story, "The Black Aeroplane," focusing on the pilot's experience of being trapped in a storm cloud with failing instruments, and the sudden appearance of a mysterious black aeroplane that guides him to safety.

Fill in the blank: Imagine you are driving a car at night on a highway and ______ a thick fog descends — your GPS fails, you can't see the road markings, and you don't know if you're in your lane or about to crash.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to sequence the key events of the pilot's ordeal in the storm (instrument failure, loss of orientation, sighting the black aeroplane, following it, landing safely) and explain how the setting (storm clouds, darkness, malfunctioning compass/radio) creates tension and necessitates the mysterious guide.
